summary: ```markdown # Seamless Blocking | Clo 2025.1 Features Deep Dive Hey everyone, it's Phoebe here, and I have an amazing new update for you called Seamless Blocking. It's going to allow you to create and drop in different textures on one pattern, so no longer do you have to cut patterns. It's really cool, and I can't wait to show it to you, so let's dive on in and have some fun while we learn. ## Introduction to Seamless Blocking Okay, so here's my Clo screen. Now, let's first break down all the ways in which you can create these things called seamless blocked lines. Just to give you guys some information, this was designed with the intent of making it so more knitwear can be possible and also so you could try to create some seamless patterns—like as close to seamless patterns as possible for knitwear. So, it's really easy to create these things, and I'm going to show you how to create them. ## Creating Seamless Blocked Lines First off, I'm going to go to my Trace Tool, which is why we call it seamless blocking. Of course, I can't wait to see all the other ways in which you use this for, but we're going to mainly focus on that for this video. ### Accessing Seamless Blocking Now, how do you get to seamless blocking? There are a few ways, and we have a few different options on how you can get there. First off, I have some internal lines here. In the Trace Tool, I can actually select these lines. I'm going to hold down Shift and select all of these internal lines, then right-click on top of one of them. Here, I'm going to see "Trace as Seamless Block Line and Shape." I'm going to select that, and now it's going to trace all of these internal lines as an internal shape. As long as all of these lines are closed shapes—meaning they go from one pattern edge to another—they will be traced as seamless blocked lines, and they all are just now. So, that's great! ### Offset as a Seamless Block Line Another way in which I can create seamless blocked lines is by using the Edit Pattern Tool. I can select a pattern outline, right-click, and now I have "Offset as Seamless Block Line." Here, I can offset it as a seamless block line. I'm going to say 1.5 and just do 4, then hit OK. I’ll do the same for this side, offsetting a seamless block line. ### Creating a New Seamless Block Line Now, I’m going to create a new seamless block line. I just have to make sure I start on a pattern piece edge and either end in a center or create something like this, which is really cool. I can also go across my half symmetry and create something interesting. ## Editing Seamless Block Lines I can go to my Edit Pattern Tool and hit delete; this is going to delete that bar for me. A seamless blocked line allows me to create those cool overlapping kinds of effects because I think that's just fun and interesting. I can also double-click to edit this. ### Managing Linked Editing Now, let me break it down for you. I went into my Edit Pattern Tool, selected it, then went over to my seamless block line, right-clicked, and now I'm going to select "Remove Linked Editing." I’m doing this because I want to delete this line but not the other. Now I have everything set for a very interesting pattern. ## Importance of Closed Shapes It must be said: a closed shape is essential for seamless blocking. I don't care how you close the shape, but it must be closed! This can be done by connecting two seamless block lines or by connecting a seamless block line to a pattern outline. It will not work if you try to close it with internal lines or baselines or if you create its own internal seamless block line. ### Examples of Closed Shapes Here’s an example of a closed shape: I connected one seamless block line to another. This is also a closed shape because it connects from a pattern outline to a pattern outline. If I try to create a seamless block line using an internal line, it will not work; it simply won't let me end it properly. ## Grading Patterns with Seamless Blocking Now, if I'm going to grade this pattern, I’m going to go into my grading tool and select this point here to add some grading. However, this grading is not going to be accurate because I am not a designer or a pattern maker. ### Seamless Lines and Grading As you can see, I'm adding grading, but the seamless lines are not getting graded. If I go to my grading and jump to medium lines, the traced internal lines will move to the sides because it always must be a closed shape. The seamless blocking doesn't disappear; it's just that you can't grade it differently. It will follow whatever the pattern outline does. **Important Note:** If you're going to edit and add grading, just know that it will follow whatever the pattern outline is doing. ## Adding Fabrics Now that we've talked about all of that, let’s get into the fun part of this and start adding some fabrics. There are several ways in which you can add in a fabric: assigning and dragging and dropping. ### Assigning Fabrics I can select a section here and hit "Assign." Oh look, it assigned! You can select like this, and it’s going to assign. Cool! ### Drag and Drop You also have this great ability to drag and drop. Look at that! Click, drag, drop. Oh my gosh, that's cool! While it might not be as cool as I initially thought, it's still pretty fun. ## Using Knitwear Feature So, here I have some knitwear. I’m going to drag and drop it here. Let me go to my back. Look at that! I added base maps to this. However, I've found that it's a little bit faster and easier for me personally to just click and assign. ### Managing Fabric Assignments Sometimes, what happens when you do what I just did is it assigns to things that you didn’t want. But it's easy to fix that by simply selecting and deleting. ## Symmetry and Seamless Blocking Now, let’s talk about symmetry. I have a half-symmetrical pattern, which normally means that if you do one thing to one side, it will happen to the other side. However, seamless blocking defies those rules. ### Breaking the Rules of Symmetry Before you think the software is broken, it’s not! We designed this intentionally so you can create a lot of different stitches, helping with knitwear that isn’t always symmetrical. ## Conclusion I’ve now created different patterns on both sides, leaning into the unsymmetrical design. I can do so many different things, and I’m really excited about how this will allow for creative freedom. Thank you all so much for watching! If you have any questions, use that comment section down below. Don’t forget to like and subscribe and check out all of our great videos on our YouTube channel. There’s a ton of information out there. Keep having fun with Clo, and I’ll see you guys in the next one. Bye! ```
